authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Six wins, one terrible loss: Mt. Silver turns to Crem
articles.dek: Josh Alakazam is out for the season. Crem Ftzpatrik delivered three touchdowns in relief as the Reds beat Cianwood 27–7.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Mt. Silver won comfortably and left with the kind of news that makes a final score feel briefly unimportant. Josh Alakazam is out for the season. The Reds are 6–0, their defense has allowed 45 points, and the quarterback who helped put them there now carries a 16-week absence on the injury report. A week after losing Garshawn Lynch, Connor McLarren has another central piece to replace.

Crem Ftzpatrik gave him a useful place to start. The Alcremie completed 15 of 18 passes for 135 yards and two touchdowns, added a one-yard rushing score, and helped finish a 27–7 win at Cianwood. There was an interception and there were three sacks. There was also a team continuing to function after an afternoon changed beneath it. Both parts belong in the account.
I'd rather Josh were answering these questions. I'm glad we got the win. The receivers made it much easier to say the calls out loud and get on with them.
body.speaker: Crem Ftzpatrik

body.text: Alakazam had been perfect through the air: seven attempts, seven completions, 56 yards. His final passing line includes a four-yard touchdown to Vibrava on fourth-and-three with 2:03 left in the first quarter. That aggressive finish gave Mt. Silver a 7–0 lead. The game report does not identify the precise injury play, and there is no reason to attach the injury to that touchdown merely because it was the most memorable thing he did.

What the record does show is the transfer of responsibility. In the second quarter, with 2:21 remaining, Ftzpatrik threw short right to Ariados for a 14-yard touchdown. The Reds led 14–0. A Stunky recovery of Bibarel's fumble earlier in the quarter had given the defense its own contribution to the change in momentum. Cianwood was being asked to catch up against a team that could still complete ordinary passes.
The receivers made room

Plusico Buress caught all eight of his targets for 54 yards. Tony Gyarzalez caught all six of his for 50. Those are strikingly unglamorous totals beside such clean catch counts, and that is why they matter. The Reds had two dependable destinations helping turn available throws into finished plays. Ftzpatrik did not have to throw for 300 yards to keep his first extended assignment moving.

Buress also had something of his own to answer. His late fumble was part of the danger in the previous week's 24–20 escape at Oreburgh. This time the Reds lost no fumbles. He did not score, but he did complete every catch the offense asked of him. A receiver can make a quarterback feel less alone without producing a spectacular play.
Throw it to me. That's what I wanted him to hear. I can't fix what happened to Josh, and I can't replay last week. I can catch the next one.
body.speaker: Plusico Buress

body.text: The running game helped, too. Raticate carried ten times for 66 yards, while Vibrava added 27 on seven attempts. Mt. Silver finished with 103 rushing yards on 22 carries. With Lynch still facing five more weeks out, those supporting contributions will become a regular subject rather than a footnote. The Reds have now had to redistribute both the throws and the handoffs.

Cianwood did make the substitute uncomfortable. Beedrill sacked Ftzpatrik twice and Victreebel once. Golbat intercepted a deep-left throw with 38 seconds left before halftime. That sequence is a fair warning against treating a successful relief appearance as an instant solution to every future problem. There will be throws to reconsider and protection work to do before Petalburg arrives.

The defense kept those mistakes affordable. Cianwood managed 183 total yards, converted three of eleven third downs, and did not score until 1:23 remained in the fourth quarter. Gardevoir's late eight-yard touchdown to Doduo reduced the margin after the Reds had already built a 27–0 lead. The Crushers fell to 2–4; a competitive stretch of their season has become an increasingly expensive collection of losses.
An unbeaten team with a new assignment

Ftzpatrik's one-yard run on third-and-one, with 48 seconds left in the third quarter, made it 20–0 before the missed extra point. In the fourth, Machamp intercepted Gardevoir, and Ftzpatrik later found Raticate for an eight-yard score to the right. The relief quarterback's touchdowns came through two different receivers and his own short run. The ball still had several ways to reach the end zone.

McLarren's immediate task is to preserve that breadth. Petalburg is 5–1 and has just held Mauville to nine points. The next opponent will have a full week to consider the quarterback it is likely to face. A successful afternoon against Cianwood gives the Reds evidence that they can compete with Ftzpatrik. It does not give them permission to ask him to become Alakazam by the next kickoff.

There is a particular cruelty in the timing. Last week's headline said the next six weeks had become harder. Now the change reaches beyond the halfback position and beyond that period. Mt. Silver still owns every win it earned, still leads its conference's playoff order, and still has a defense capable of making a modest offensive day sufficient. Those advantages are real, and they are worth protecting while the offense learns a different rhythm.

Ftzpatrik does not have to make the whole season understandable at once. His first answer was a short-right touchdown to Ariados. His last was another to Raticate. Between them, the Reds found enough football to get to six wins.

articles.title: Ninety-four yards. Then ninety-four more.
articles.dek: My Way, Son returned two kickoffs for touchdowns, ran for 118 yards and helped Rustboro turn Dewford's big plays into a 37–21 defeat.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Dewford scored the sort of touchdown that should change a game: a 96-yard interception return by Gligar with one second left in the first quarter. Rustboro answered on the next kickoff. Then Dewford scored again in the second quarter, and Rustboro answered on that kickoff, too. Both returns traveled 94 yards. Both belonged to My Way, Son. The Breakers kept finding the end zone and then losing the benefit before their defense could get comfortable.

Rustboro won 37–21 behind an Iron Treads performance that makes a normal all-purpose line look insufficient. My Way, Son ran eighteen times for 118 yards, caught two passes for 45, and returned three kicks for 226 with two touchdowns. Add those yards and you get 389. The total includes returns, of course, but Dewford still had to defend every one of them.
The second one still needed the blocks. I know people will see the two numbers and talk about me. I saw the lanes, and I tried to stay patient long enough to use them.
body.speaker: My Way, Son

body.text: Tyler Scarboro's club needed a result with some force behind it. A week earlier, Rustboro lost 12–10 to Pewter despite Philly's 97 rushing yards. Four field goals beat an offense that had done enough between the lines and too little with its chances. This time the Stone scored 24 points in the second quarter alone. The final whistle brought them to 3–3 and pushed them into sixth place in the Hoenn–Sinnoh playoff order.
Dewford could not keep a lead

The opening was hardly tidy. Shieldon lost a fumble after a short-right completion in the first quarter, and Frosmoth then threw the interception that Gligar took almost the entire length of the field. Rustboro had given away two possessions before it had scored. The seven-point deficit at the quarter break was small compared with how damaging the sequence could have felt.

Numel's kickoff opened the second quarter. My Way, Son took it 94 yards for a touchdown, and Gorebyss's extra point tied the game. At 3:08, Dewford's Frosmoth threw deep left to Watchog for a 41-yard score. Numel converted, kicked off, and watched the same Iron Treads go the same distance again. The score was tied at fourteen after a second return that was every bit as costly as the first.

There is no useful way to soften that for Brawly. Two scoring plays had created two opportunities to defend a lead. Neither opportunity survived the kickoff. Dewford could still make a spectacular play, but its coverage unit kept requiring another one. A team already missing Excadrill and Ambipom did not need to keep restarting its offensive work from a level score.

Rustboro finally moved ahead through its passing game. Frosmoth found Gengar deep right for an eighteen-yard touchdown with 1:03 left in the half. Gorebyss added a 43-yard field goal with twelve seconds remaining. A quarter that began with the Stone trailing 7–0 ended with them leading 24–14. The return touchdowns changed the pace, and the offense used the extra breathing room.

Gengar's appearance also belongs to this week's story. The former Haunter is now back with Rustboro after the trade-related evolution, and the recorded scoring play names Gengar. There is no need to turn the sequence into a new destination or a permanent departure. The relevant sight for Dewford was a receiver in Rustboro's offense finishing an eighteen-yard touchdown.
The ground game stayed on the field

The Stone did not spend the second half waiting for another return. They finished with 222 rushing yards on 37 carries. Philly contributed eighty yards and a touchdown on twelve attempts, while My Way, Son supplied the larger share. Rustboro converted seven of ten third downs. Dewford converted none of six. That difference kept one offense working and sent the other looking for another sudden answer.

Armaldo recovered two Dewford fumbles in the third quarter, one after a completion to Boldore and another after an Unfezant run. Frosmoth scored on a three-yard run with 2:13 left in that quarter. In the fourth, Milotic intercepted a deep-right pass and returned it 26 yards. Philly's three-yard touchdown at 3:48 pushed the lead to 37–14 before the missed extra point.
Ninety-four twice is showing off. I had three yards to get and got them. They all go on the same scoreboard, so I'm happy to let him do the long commute.
body.speaker: Philly

body.text: Dewford's late two-yard touchdown run by Pidgeotto made the final margin sixteen. The Breakers still finished with only seven first downs against Rustboro's twenty-two, and their 219 total yards were well behind the Stone's 365. The return story is enormous, but it should not conceal how much ordinary possession football Rustboro won after the early mistakes.

There was a substantial cost on defense. Parasect is listed out for five weeks after this game. That matters for a team trying to turn a .500 record into sustained progress rather than another weekly reversal. Azalea is next, fresh from a second consecutive win. Rustboro cannot assume that a pair of kickoff touchdowns will travel with it.

For Dewford, now also 3–3, the trip to Olivine carries a more immediate question. The Breakers have lost a game in which they produced a 96-yard defensive touchdown and a 41-yard passing score. The repair starts with the moments after they score. Twice against Rustboro, the celebration lasted only as long as Numel's kickoff.

articles.title: Four touchdowns, no punts: Ninjaskamara keeps Mossdeep rolling
articles.dek: A 213-yard day from scrimmage and a suffocating run defense carried the Eclipse past Lavaridge, 41–3, to 6–0.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: The most revealing eight seconds of Mossdeep's 41–3 win came just before halftime. With 37 seconds left, Lavaridge faced fourth-and-two and Delphox was sacked by DurrickBurgess. With 29 seconds left, Dram Marino threw deep left to Ninjaskamara for a forty-yard touchdown. A possible Inferno drive became seven Eclipse points almost immediately. Mossdeep's offense did not need to be asked twice.

Ninjaskamara finished with four touchdowns: three rushing and one receiving. His twelve carries produced exactly one hundred yards; his four catches produced 113 more. The Eclipse improved to 6–0, stretched their season scoring margin to plus-201, and gave Lavaridge a second straight week without a touchdown. The final was comprehensive even though the opening quarter had ended tied at three.

On the pass, I wanted to secure it before I thought about the finish. You get a chance like that after the defense makes a play, you don't want to give the chance back. The run scores were the same idea: find what is there, keep the ball safe.
body.speaker: Ninjaskamara

body.text: Marino completed nineteen of 33 passes for 262 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. He was not sacked. Mossdeep did not punt. The offense produced twenty first downs and 456 total yards, with 194 coming on the ground. There were incomplete throws and early drives that ended in field goals, but the Eclipse kept enough possessions alive to make those imperfections relatively inexpensive.

Adam Vinathorn opened the scoring with a 55-yard field goal at 4:30 in the first quarter. Lavaridge answered through Charjabug from fifty yards with 1:47 left. That was the last time the Inferno scored. Vinathorn's 25-yard kick early in the second put Mossdeep back ahead, and Ninjaskamara's three-yard run up the middle at 2:55 supplied the first touchdown.
The halfback was not alone

Marshall Flock had the same number of carries as Ninjaskamara and gained 77 yards. After last week's two-return-touchdown feature, Flock's contribution was quieter and thoroughly useful. Mossdeep could keep handing the ball off without asking one runner to supply every yard. Ninjulio Jones added nineteen yards on two rushes, while Marino's two kneels accounted for the small subtraction at the bottom of the team total.

Gronkaludon caught four passes for 57 yards. Ninjulio caught four for 33. Travis Meltce added 23 on two catches, and both Lorenzo Steel and Vita Weba contributed fourteen receiving yards. The offense found several short gains around Ninjaskamara's explosive catches. Its longest reception was a 48-yarder by the halfback; the scoring catch before halftime went forty. They were different plays, and Lavaridge had to survive both.

I liked the carries. Last week everybody wanted to talk about the returns, which was nice. This week I got to help keep us moving. If he's finishing the drives, I'm fine being one of the reasons we got there.
body.speaker: Marshall Flock

body.text: The offensive line supplied a particularly clean platform. Gene Shuckshaw and Shuck Bednarik each recorded nine pancakes and a 100 percent block-win figure. Bastony Boseli recorded twelve pancakes. Those numbers do not require the invention of a particular blocking assignment on a particular touchdown. Alongside zero sacks allowed, they describe an afternoon in which the ball carriers and quarterback had considerable help.

The Conkeldurr in the pivotal sack was another change worth recognizing. DurrickBurgess had completed his trade evolution before this game and appeared in the recorded play as Conkeldurr. The defensive box score divides that sack credit, giving him half a sack and Shawn Mareman half. The play log names the finisher; the individual totals preserve the shared credit. Both show a defense ending the possession when Lavaridge needed two yards.
Fifteen rushing yards, zero third-down conversions

Lavaridge's problems began before the passing downs. Swampert managed ten yards on eight carries, with a long gain of ten. The Inferno finished with fifteen rushing yards on eleven attempts. Derrat Brooks recorded ten tackles and four tackles for loss. Mossdeep repeatedly made a small rushing workload produce almost nothing, leaving Delphox to keep finding completions without a dependable second route forward.

Delphox did complete seventeen of 26 passes for 172 yards and threw no interceptions. Staravia caught eight for 63. Those are respectable individual fragments inside a team performance that produced no third-down conversions in seven attempts. Clay Rathews recorded two sacks, and the Inferno lost a fumble after a fourth-quarter completion to Tropius. Luvrelle Revis recovered it. Lavaridge finished with eight first downs.

Ninjaskamara's six-yard run to the right with 2:55 left in the third quarter made it 27–3 after the extra point. His nine-yard run up the middle at the start of the fourth supplied his fourth touchdown of the day. Poury Holt later caught an eight-yard pass to the left on third-and-three for the final touchdown. The Eclipse kept scoring without needing a return or interception touchdown to enlarge the margin.

Lavaridge fell to 2–4 and now travels to Blackthorn. Mantine is listed out for two weeks after the loss, adding a secondary problem to a difficult stretch. Mossdeep goes to Lavender, which had a bye and remains 4–1. That will ask a different question of Michael Dorrill's team than two consecutive home wins by a combined ninety points to six.

The Eclipse can take this much with them: no punts, no sacks allowed, no turnovers, and four touchdowns from a halfback who required only sixteen touches from scrimmage. Lavender has a week of rest. It will need a plan for number twenty-seven.

articles.title: Venomoth finds 69 yards of breathing room
articles.dek: Saffron survived Fuchsia 16–14 after a late deep strike, five sacks and a final possession that never went back to the Shadows.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron spent most of this game looking like a team that had misplaced its comfortable win. Then Venomoth found it, sixty-nine yards down the right side. Archiekazam's touchdown pass with 3:44 left in the fourth quarter gave the Psi Corps just enough room to survive Fuchsia 16–14. The room was promptly reduced, but it was never completely taken away.

The result leaves Saffron 5–1 and Fuchsia 0–6. The experience was much closer than those records suggest. The Shadows outgained the Psi Corps 270–267, collected thirteen first downs to ten, and converted six of fourteen third downs. Saffron converted none of four. If you arrived expecting another version of last week's 48–0 win over Lavaridge, you were following the wrong script by the fourth quarter.
The score made that throw important, but I wanted the read to stay the same. We had the chance to the right. Venomoth finished it. After that, the job was getting the next possession right, too.
body.speaker: Archiekazam

body.text: Archiekazam completed eleven of fifteen passes for 174 yards and two touchdowns without an interception. Venomoth caught both of his targets for 98 yards. HeeDee Lamb caught all four of his for 39 and the other touchdown. There was efficiency when Saffron actually threw, but the offense did not get enough sustained work to make its early lead comfortable.

Lamb's nine-yard touchdown catch to the left, with 2:51 remaining in the first quarter, opened the scoring. Gorebyss added a 44-yard field goal early in the second. At 10–0, Saffron had the lead, the pass rush and the reputation. It did not have an afternoon that could be safely filed away. Vigoroth's second-quarter fumble, recovered by Cacturne, was one reason the distance stayed manageable.
The sacks bought time

Fuchsia's Empoleon completed 25 of thirty throws for 204 yards and two touchdowns. That completion rate makes the five sacks stand out even more. Saffron did not spend the day intercepting him; neither quarterback threw a pick. The defense instead took yards and possessions away before the completed passes could become enough points.

Watchog supplied a first-quarter sack on third-and-three. Verrick Brooks, the Victreebel wearing number 52, added two sacks in the first half. Pawmo got another on third-and-eight before the break. Kecleon brought Empoleon down on third-and-nine in the third quarter. Those five plays cost Fuchsia 33 yards, and three of the sacks explicitly came on third down. The pressure was doing work the final two-point margin can obscure.

The Shadows kept coming anyway. Oinkologne ran thirteen times for 58 yards and caught four passes for 27. Heatmor had 49 receiving yards, Gumshoos 37, and a broad collection of short targets kept Empoleon's completion total climbing. Fuchsia did not need one receiver to overpower the game. It needed enough of those completed throws to become scores before the clock disappeared.

The first touchdown finally arrived with 4:09 left, when Empoleon threw short right to Palpitoad for six yards on third-and-four. The extra point made it 10–7. Saffron answered within the next minute: Archiekazam threw deep right to Venomoth on second-and-nine, and the receiver went 69 yards for the touchdown that restored a nine-point lead. Gorebyss missed the extra point, so nine was all the cushion Saffron had.
I was glad the ball came my way. He gave me a good throw, and I wanted to finish it for him. We still had work after the score. Nobody on their side had decided to stop.
body.speaker: Venomoth

body.text: Fourteen points were real pressure

Fuchsia's second touchdown came on fourth-and-seven. Empoleon found Weepinbell short right for thirteen yards with 2:09 remaining, and Clamperl's extra point cut it to 16–14. It was an impressive conversion under a demand that could not be postponed. The Shadows had turned a game with almost three scoreless quarters into a finish where one more possession might matter.

They did not get that possession. At the two-minute warning, Saffron had second-and-one. Watchog ran right for five, then up the middle for seven. Archiekazam completed a fourteen-yard pass to Watchog on second-and-three. The quarterback could then kneel twice. The final stretch was a sequence of practical gains by the same player who had helped start the pass rush much earlier.

Gorebyss finished one-for-two on field goals and one-for-two on extra points. Fuchsia missed its only field-goal attempt. Those lost points belong in the explanation, but neither side can solve the game by casually adding its misses to the score. Saffron still had to earn the final first downs. Fuchsia still had to reach those fourth-quarter touchdown chances after absorbing five sacks.

Trent Scarboro also takes an injury concern into the bye: Vigoroth is listed out for three weeks. He had carried ten times for 73 yards, a productive line alongside the lost fumble. His absence changes the distribution of useful rushing work, and the bye gives Saffron time to consider it. Fuchsia hosts Veilstone next while still missing Sharpedo, listed out four weeks.

For the Psi Corps, this was a win worth keeping and a performance worth correcting. For the Shadows, it was their strongest argument in a while that the next close finish need not end like the others. The difference this time was sixty-nine yards to Venomoth, followed by three gains from Watchog that kept the ball away.

articles.title: Sunyshore gets its returns the right way round
articles.dek: Pat Serptain's 63-yard punt touchdown and Fred Whirler's late pick-six powered a 34–7 response to last week's loss.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore had spent a week on the wrong side of a return story. Against Veilstone, the Starseekers wrote two of their own. Pat Serptain took a punt 63 yards for a touchdown early in the third quarter. Fred Whirler returned an interception thirteen yards for another late in the fourth. A 34–7 win moved Sunyshore to 5–1 and gave Karson Jones something considerably more pleasant to discuss than Milotic's previous visit.

The defense made the response convincing. Veilstone gained 115 total yards, managed five first downs and converted one of thirteen third downs. Tatsugiri threw two interceptions and was sacked four times. The Fists had one scoring drive, following their own interception, and very little sustained offense around it. Sunyshore did not need its attack to be flawless to take control.

That distinction matters because the Starseekers did punt five times. DeZhaun Watzon threw an interception, and the offense converted only three of nine third downs. The final margin should not be mistaken for an afternoon of uninterrupted offensive efficiency. Sunyshore won with a passing game that finished chances, a return game that supplied a touchdown, and a defense that kept creating another opportunity.

A punt is a very polite invitation to borrow the football. I thought sixty-three yards was a reasonable borrowing distance. The blockers might ask for their share of the credit, and they would be right.
body.speaker: Pat Serptain

body.text: The first fourteen came through the air

Watzon completed nineteen of 31 passes for 162 yards and three touchdowns. The first two went to the receiver recorded as Buizel in the game, who has since evolved into Floatzel. The identity is the same player; the game-day catches happened as Buizel. He finished with six receptions for 55 yards and two scores, a compact line with a substantial effect on the scoreboard.

The opening touchdown was a seven-yard pass deep left with 3:18 left in the first quarter. The second was a one-yard pass short left with 31 seconds remaining in the half. Duosion made both extra points, and Sunyshore led 14–0 at the break. The offense had not run away in yardage, but it had converted two possessions into the largest available return.

Myles Gabite carried six times for 38 yards. BAXXED? added fifteen on four attempts, and Scol Alexander contributed six on two. Sunyshore finished with 65 rushing yards on seventeen carries, including Watzon's running and late kneels. Sceptile caught five passes for 46 yards, while Fera LaGatr had four for 34 and the third passing touchdown. The attack had several supporting pieces even with the modest total of 227 yards.

After halftime, the defense quickly returned Veilstone to its punter. Conkeldurr sacked Tatsugiri for seven yards on second-and-ten. At 5:15, Sunflora punted fifty yards to the Sunyshore 37. Serptain took the ball the remaining 63 yards for the touchdown, and the extra point made it 21–0. He finished with six returns for 125 yards. One of them had done most of the damage.

The Fists briefly found a route back when Corviknight intercepted Watzon's deep-left pass and returned it twenty yards. Palpitoad completed the subsequent scoring chance with a five-yard run up the middle late in the third quarter. At 21–7, Veilstone had finally scored and had evidence that the opposing quarterback could give it another opening. The next interception, however, went the other way.
The fourth quarter belonged to the defense

Jolt Vick intercepted Tatsugiri's short-left throw on third-and-eleven with 5:10 remaining and returned it 44 yards. Watzon later found Fera LaGatr short left for a nine-yard touchdown. Duosion missed the extra point, leaving the score 27–7. The interception had supplied the kind of change in field position that made a modest passing total much more effective.

Whirler completed the scoring at 1:46. Facing fourth-and-eleven, Tatsugiri threw short middle and the Poliwrath took the interception thirteen yards into the end zone. Whirler's defensive line included five tackles, two tackles for loss, four pressures and that touchdown. It was an emphatic finish to a day in which Veilstone rarely escaped the next difficult down.
I wanted the ball. Once I had it, I wanted the end zone. We had done too much work putting them in those downs to let the last part of the game get soft.
body.speaker: Fred Whirler

body.text: Torten Carter recorded two sacks, with the other two supplied by Conkeldurr and Dragonair. Veilstone's Whiscash managed thirteen rushing yards on sixteen carries. That combination explains why the Fists kept arriving at situations where a short completion was unlikely to be sufficient. Even their final possession contained two more sacks before a six-yard completion on fourth-and-26 ended it.

The win does not erase last week's 33–20 loss to Violet or answer every question about Sunyshore's consistency. It does show a team capable of directing the next game rather than extending the previous one's frustration. The Starseekers now have a plus-95 scoring margin and sit second in the Hoenn–Sinnoh playoff order. Cerulean, coming off a 20–3 defeat at Vermilion, is next on the road.

Veilstone fell to 3–3 and travels to Fuchsia, where the winless Shadows have just taken Saffron to a two-point finish. That opponent will look at one conversion in thirteen third-down tries and believe there is a game to win. Sunyshore can look at Serptain's punt return and Whirler's interception and enjoy a simpler conclusion: this week, the return touchdowns belonged to them.

articles.title: Lavender's first job: make Mossdeep punt
articles.dek: The Eclipse have plenty of spectacular numbers. Mara Voss starts with the possession that ended at 0:37 and the touchdown that followed eight seconds later.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I want Lavender to make Mossdeep punt before anyone starts telling me what this matchup means for the Indigo Bowl. One punt. A normal, recognizable change of possession in which Dram Marino has to leave the field because the defense finished its assignment. Lavaridge never managed it. Until an opponent can produce that ordinary inconvenience, the grander discussion is mostly giving the Eclipse something pleasant to read.

Mossdeep scored 41 points, gained 456 yards and handed Ninjaskamara four touchdowns' worth of work. Those are easy numbers to admire. The number I keep returning to is zero in the punt column. Michael Dorrill's offense had incomplete passes, settled for two field goals and did not convert every third down. It still never handed the Inferno a routine punt possession. That's an enormous amount of control over the afternoon.

I wrote last week that I enjoyed the other 46 points in the 49–3 win over Fuchsia, too. Fine. I still do. This week I want to discuss why the points kept arriving without the assistance of a return touchdown. The answer is in a combination that should worry Travis Scarboro: the Eclipse can win a short-yardage exchange on defense and immediately refuse to play short-yardage football on offense.

With 37 seconds left in the first half, Lavaridge faced fourth-and-two. Delphox was sacked. The play names DurrickBurgess, now a Conkeldurr; the individual box score splits the sack between him and Shawn Mareman. Either way, the possession ended. Eight seconds later Marino threw deep left to Ninjaskamara for a forty-yard touchdown. A defense made one decisive stop, and its offense treated the next snap as a chance to take the whole field.

That is the sequence I would put first in Lavender's preparation. There is no reason to invent an offensive formation or a coverage mistake the record doesn't identify. The documented choice is enough: first-and-ten, deep left, forty yards, touchdown. Mossdeep did not use the late possession merely to collect a few harmless yards and consider a kick. It had a halfback who could finish a deep pass.
I don't want the clock to make me careless. But if the throw is there, passing it up is a decision, too. He gave us a chance to finish the half with seven. The protection let me take it.
body.speaker: Dram Marino

body.text: Stop calling the whole thing a running game

Ninjaskamara ran for one hundred yards and caught passes for 113. Calling him a rushing threat captures less than half his yardage in this game. The forty-yard touchdown wasn't even his longest reception; he also had a 48-yard catch. Lavender's problem is a player who can turn a handoff into a score up the middle, take a run right for another, and then make the defense defend a deep pass to the left.

That does not mean the rest of the offense can be ignored. Marshall Flock had twelve carries, the same as Ninjaskamara, and gained 77 yards. Gronkaludon caught four for 57. Seven Mossdeep players caught passes. The Eclipse can ask several different players to make the manageable gain while waiting for their best finisher to make a very large one. That's why chasing the headline player around the field is an incomplete plan.

The protection is the other part I would refuse to discuss vaguely. Marino was not sacked. Gene Shuckshaw and Shuck Bednarik each recorded a 100 percent block-win figure, and Bastony Boseli collected twelve pancakes. Those are broad game totals, not proof of who blocked whom on the forty-yard score. They still tell Lavender that creating pressure will require something more persuasive than hoping a talented front eventually gets through.

At the other end, Derrat Brooks made ten tackles and four tackles for loss. Lavaridge ran eleven times for fifteen yards and failed on all seven third-down attempts. I get impatient when a blowout becomes a conversation exclusively about offensive glamour. Mossdeep's defense repeatedly created situations where the Inferno had to find the answer through Delphox, then ended enough of those possessions to keep the entire game moving in one direction.
A fair test for a rested opponent

Lavender brings a 4–1 record and a bye into this game. It also brings a season scoring margin of plus-one. I am not dismissing the four wins; the Wails earned them. I am asking what kind of contest they have to build to earn a fifth. A wide-open exchange against a team with 244 points in six games seems an unnecessarily generous invitation. The first target should be fewer Mossdeep possessions that end in points.

My checkable standard is three Eclipse punts and no Mossdeep completion of thirty yards or more. That is a demanding combination, and it is meant to be. If Lavender can repeatedly end possessions and remove the giant pass from the scorebook, its own offense gets a game it can manage. If it cannot, a close fourth-quarter script may never become available. Rest helps a team prepare; it doesn't award any first downs.

For Mossdeep, I want the same discipline that made this win so severe: no giveaways and protection that holds up when the opponent knows what is coming. The Eclipse's two most recent wins total ninety points scored and six allowed. There is no need to manufacture an argument that those games were secretly difficult. There is a need to recognize that Lavender will arrive with a different opportunity and a full week to study the methods.

I would begin that study with the fourth-and-two at 0:37. Then I would play the next snap. I would let the room see Ninjaskamara finish the forty yards, and I would ask the defense how it plans to prevent the next version. The answer has to be better than hoping Mossdeep finally feels like punting.

art.alt: Ninjaskamara, Ninjask No. 27, carrying a football in Mossdeep magenta and gold.

articles.title: Let Crem be Crem
articles.dek: Mt. Silver's replacement quarterback does not owe anyone an imitation. Ellis Quill on the useful, modest things that made a difficult afternoon survivable.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: I don't think Crem Ftzpatrik owes Mt. Silver a convincing impression of Josh Alakazam. I think he owes it the next sensible throw. That sounds like an awfully small ambition for a 6–0 team, but an unbeaten record can make the people around a new quarterback ask for everything at once. Ftzpatrik did enough against Cianwood to deserve a week without being assigned somebody else's personality, arm or future.

Alakazam is out for the season, with sixteen weeks listed on the injury report. Garshawn Lynch remains out for five more. The Reds have spent consecutive victories losing players who helped make those victories seem likely. There is something particularly disorienting about winning while the season keeps changing shape. The standings tell you to celebrate. The next day's preparation tells you to begin again in several important places.

Ftzpatrik completed fifteen of eighteen passes for 135 yards, threw two touchdowns, and scored another on a one-yard run. He also threw an interception and took three sacks. I like that the complete line resists an instant fairy tale. A reserve came in and did useful work. Some of it was difficult. Some of it went wrong. The team won 27–7, and he can study the mistakes without having to carry a defeat along with them.
I don't really know what to say when people ask if this is my moment. Josh got hurt. I wanted to help. I'll be happier talking about a good throw than making it sound like I was waiting for that.
body.speaker: Crem Ftzpatrik

body.text: That seems a reasonable distinction to me. It also gives Connor McLarren a reasonable starting point. He can prepare the player he actually has, in the offense that is actually available, while recognizing how much the surrounding team contributed. The Reds allowed only seven points. Their runners gained 103 yards. Their receivers caught several modest passes that kept the offense from turning every new down into a new emergency.

Plusico Buress caught eight balls on eight targets. Tony Gyarzalez caught six on six. Together they supplied 104 receiving yards without a touchdown. I suspect those lines will be read quickly beneath the quarterback news. They deserve a longer pause. A replacement quarterback can be helped enormously by a receiver who finishes the available catch rather than requiring a perfect dramatic throw to contribute.
The useful apology is the next catch

Buress had been part of the trouble at Oreburgh the week before. His late fumble made that 24–20 escape more dangerous. Against Cianwood, the Reds did not lose a fumble. I am wary of calling every better afternoon redemption, as though a professional life is a collection of little courtroom scenes. Still, eight catches on eight chances is a fairly good way to answer an uncomfortable week.
I wanted him to throw with confidence. If that means eight ordinary catches, give me eight ordinary catches. I'll take them. Last week is there. It doesn't get to catch this week's football for me.
body.speaker: Plusico Buress

body.text: Ftzpatrik found Ariados for a fourteen-yard touchdown to the right in the second quarter and Raticate for eight to the same side in the fourth. Between them he scored on a one-yard run. I am not reading an entire offensive identity into three scoring plays. I am observing that the Reds found scores through several players and several kinds of work. They did not simply wait for a single replacement star to appear.

The interception belongs here, too. Golbat took the deep-left pass late in the first half. Beedrill and Victreebel supplied the sacks. The relief appearance was successful without being protected from unpleasant moments. That is more encouraging to me than a story in which every mistake is hidden behind the victory. A player who finishes the game after a bad throw has at least begun the work of handling the next one.

Mt. Silver's defense helped set the emotional temperature. Cianwood scored with 1:23 remaining, after the Reds had built a 27–0 lead. Before that, the Crushers lost a Bibarel fumble recovered by Stunky and a Gardevoir interception caught by Machamp. The defense gave the offense the sort of margin in which a cautious decision could remain merely cautious. Ftzpatrik was not asked to rescue a collapsing scoreboard on every possession.
Petalburg will ask something new

The next opponent is 5–1 Petalburg. The Pride just beat Mauville 21–9 and will have an opportunity to prepare for Ftzpatrik from the beginning. That changes the assignment. A relief quarterback enters a game already in motion; a likely starter becomes part of the other team's week's work. The Reds cannot know how that will go by looking only at a completion percentage from Cianwood.

They can know what helped. Raticate's ten carries for 66 yards helped. Vibrava's 27 yards helped. Buress and Gyarzalez finishing their catches helped. McLarren can build the next week's conversation around those contributions rather than beginning with a list of things Alakazam would have done. A missing starter leaves a large absence. Repeating the dimensions of that absence does not fill it.

I am not ready to move Mt. Silver out of the contender discussion. Six wins, a plus-109 margin and 45 points allowed are substantial accomplishments. I am also not ready to declare the quarterback problem solved because one afternoon ended well. Both reactions would make the story easier to tell than the season is likely to be. The Reds have earned a cushion; now they have to use it intelligently.

Ftzpatrik's first extended answer was modest enough to be believable: completed passes, two touchdown throws, a short scoring run, and a few errors the defense could withstand. I would let him keep that version of the afternoon. When Petalburg arrives, the first useful thing he can do is find an available receiver and put the ball where that receiver can catch it.

art.alt: Silver and red quarterback helmets numbered 7 and 12 beside a football.

articles.title: Eighteen carries. One hundred eight yards. Thank you.
articles.dek: Dorian Pike asked Cinnabar to pick up the ball. The Blaze answered with 27 points, a division win and a much more convincing running game.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Blaine, I would like to begin with a sincere expression of gratitude. Your football team carried the football eighteen times. It gained 108 yards. It scored two rushing touchdowns. It beat Pewter 27–10. These are beautiful, uncomplicated numbers, and I am prepared to admire them at considerable volume. Last week I asked Cinnabar to pick up the ball. This week Cinnabar picked it up and took it somewhere.

I know. The passing game had another productive afternoon. Gholdengo threw for 221 yards, Frogadier caught seven passes for 105, and Exploud caught seven for 69. I have eyes. I can enjoy those things while also noticing that a team with a useful quarterback became substantially harder to inconvenience when its rushing total stopped looking like a misplaced receiving line.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the Blaze needed this response. Twelve carries for twenty-five yards in the previous loss at Dewford was a poor way to support a passing game capable of making an opponent defend the field. Eighteen for 108 against Pewter is six yards a carry. Six. You do not need a complicated speech to understand what six yards does for the next down.

Seismitoad led it with ten carries for 69 yards and a touchdown. Gholdengo added 22 on five and scored from two yards out. Pidgeotto supplied seventeen on three. Three different contributors, a sensible amount of work, and enough production to make a defender care about the handoff. I am not asking for a museum exhibit of old football. I am asking for an offense that presents more than one unpleasant choice.
I was happy they kept giving me chances. The blockers did a lot for me. If a run helps the next pass, that's good work, too. I don't need every useful carry to be the one that scores.
body.speaker: Seismitoad

body.text: Very gracious. Very considerate. Allow me to be less restrained on your behalf: 69 yards on ten carries is useful, and the 29-yard long gain is useful, and a five-yard touchdown up the middle early in the second quarter is useful. Cinnabar should make room for that usefulness again next week instead of treating it as a surprising guest who has to leave before dinner.
The part after thirteen to ten

The Blaze led 13–3 at halftime. Charjabug had made field goals from 51 and 24 yards, and Seismitoad had scored between them. Pewter then opened the third quarter with an eleven-yard touchdown pass from Wyrdeer to Yanmega. At 13–10, Cinnabar had reached the portion of a game where a favored team can begin behaving as if the lead itself ought to do the work.

The Blaze answered with actual work. Arcanine sacked Wyrdeer twice in the third quarter, once for eight yards and once for seven. Gholdengo scored on a two-yard run to the right with 1:45 left in the period. Octillery intercepted Wyrdeer forty-four seconds later and returned the ball nineteen yards. Cinnabar had a defense changing possessions and an offense finishing a chance on the ground.

That is how you keep a game from becoming a tribute to the opponent's resilience. You make the next useful play. Then you make another. A three-point lead became ten, and the fourth quarter brought a four-yard touchdown pass short right to Wigglytuff. One catch, one target, one touchdown. Wigglytuff contributed exactly the number of yards the situation required and declined to make the matter more complicated.

Gholdengo finished nineteen-for-31 with a touchdown, no interceptions and one sack taken. The quarterback did not need to throw every point onto the board. He could share the scoring with Seismitoad, contribute a short run himself and trust a defense that held Pewter to 199 total yards. The Blaze finished with 329. That is a substantial advantage in ordinary offensive production, and the final score reflected it.
Frogadier has been worth your attention

I also want the seven catches for 105 yards discussed properly. Frogadier caught seven of ten targets and had a long gain of 29. Those are receiving yards that repeatedly moved the offense, even though the touchdown pass went to somebody else. If you only count the names attached to scoring plays, you will miss much of the reason the Blaze were close enough to score them.
I liked being someone he could keep coming back to. The yards are nice. I would've liked to finish one in the end zone, but we got there through other guys. That was enough for this game.
body.speaker: Frogadier

body.text: Exploud's seven catches for 69 yards gave Gholdengo another reliable destination. Together those two receivers produced fourteen catches and 174 yards. The quarterback had room to move the ball through them, the runners had room to contribute, and the offense did not lose a fumble. This was a much fuller performance than a box score built around one large passing number and an apology for everything else.

The kicking was not perfect. Charjabug made two of three field goals, although all three extra points went through. There is the small piece of housekeeping I am willing to mention while enjoying a seventeen-point win. Oricorio also remains listed out for one week, so the secondary is still working around an absence. Neither fact requires pretending that the afternoon was less convincing than it was.

Cinnabar is 4–2 with 125 points scored, 71 allowed and a plus-54 margin. The Blaze lead the Kanto West in the current standings and hold the fourth conference playoff seed. Eterna comes next, carrying a 24–21 win at Snowpoint. That matchup gives Blaine another chance to demonstrate that the improved running game can remain part of the weekly offense, rather than an answer delivered once to shut up a columnist.
It did not shut up the columnist. Obviously.

I want Seismitoad involved again. I want the quarterback protected, Frogadier targeted and the defense finishing its pressure with the kind of sacks Arcanine supplied. The Blaze have just shown how all of those things can fit inside the same win. Eighteen carries. One hundred eight yards. Put those numbers where the next game plan can see them.

articles.title: The Rook Board: Meowth makes me choose the athlete
articles.dek: Seviper owns the strongest grade band. Central Sinnoh’s Meowth owns the movement tests. Calvin Rook ranks twelve receivers from a group of twenty-one.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Central Sinnoh’s Meowth is my first receiver. Celadon’s Seviper has the stronger present grade band, and I expect plenty of sensible scouts to prefer him. I am taking the 4.71 forty, 43-inch vertical and 6.27 cone seriously enough to put the athlete first. This is a scouting opinion with an obvious argument against it. Keep both parts of the sentence.

This week’s circuit covers the twenty listed WRs and one SLOT, with twelve prospects on the board. Grades remain ranges; combines describe the workout. They do not tell us a receiver’s college production, guarantee an evolution or promise a future starting job. The useful question is which actual assignment a team would be buying.

Rustboro just received an eighteen-yard touchdown from Gengar. Saffron survived because Venomoth finished a 69-yard pass. Those plays explain why teams keep looking for receiving threats. They do not make every prospect of a related species the next version of an established player. I want a fit, a price and a job before I want a comparison that sounds good on draft night.

prospects.name: Meowth
prospects.analysis: I am putting Central Sinnoh’s Meowth first, and I know exactly which objection is coming: the 41–69 grade band is lower than several others. The movement testing wins me over. A 4.71 forty, 43-inch vertical and 6.27 cone are the best marks in this receiver group. That is the athlete I want to investigate first when I need a receiver to create space.
prospects.concern: Ten bench reps do not settle how he handles contact, and the broad grade band leaves real uncertainty about present receiving polish.
prospects.projection: My first receiver target for Fortree, whose 0–5 start demands a stronger offensive future. This is a fit opinion, not a forecast of its draft slot.

prospects.name: Seviper
prospects.analysis: Seviper offers the strongest current grade band here at 62–90 and nineteen bench reps. Celadon’s prospect gives a club a different reason to be interested than Meowth does: there is a stronger present evaluation range and a much sturdier strength result. I would be entirely comfortable with a team reversing my top two because it values that combination more.
prospects.concern: The 4.95 forty and 6.87 cone trail the leading movement testers. The strongest band is still a band, not a completed scouting report.
prospects.projection: A receiver-needy club wanting a more immediate contribution should start here. I would put Cerulean on the list after its three-point afternoon.

prospects.name: Gastly
prospects.analysis: Sycamore’s Gastly pairs a 4.82 forty with a 6.53 cone and a 41-inch vertical. The 57–85 band belongs near the top, too. I like how little explaining is required to make the movement case. Think about the stress a receiver can place on a defense when it must respect both the initial acceleration and a change of direction.
prospects.concern: Four bench reps are the clearest weakness in the testing profile. Movement alone does not establish dependable receiving or blocking work.
prospects.projection: A serious early option for a team seeking another explosive receiving threat. Rustboro has just shown how useful a Gengar can be, without making that an automatic comparison of ability.

prospects.name: Delibird
prospects.analysis: Hulbury’s Delibird has a 56–84 grade band, a 41-inch vertical and a 6.62 cone. I see a balanced candidate to challenge for real receiving work rather than a workout attraction with one number doing all the selling. The 4.92 forty does not lead the class, but the other movement tests keep the profile interesting.
prospects.concern: Eight bench reps and a broad band leave work to do on the contact and present-skill questions. Do not turn a good jump into an invented catch history.
prospects.projection: A sensible receiver addition for an offense that already has one dependable option and needs another. Pewter should be looking at more ways to reach the end zone.

prospects.name: Chinchou
prospects.analysis: The only listed SLOT in this group belongs high enough to be discussed on his own terms. Azalea University’s Chinchou has a 56–84 band, runs 4.87 and posts a 6.70 cone. A club that has a real inside receiving job can consider those numbers without pretending every receiver has to solve the same outside assignment.
prospects.concern: A 36-inch vertical and ten bench reps do not distinguish him from every outside prospect. The role must exist before the selection makes sense.
prospects.projection: My first call for a team specifically shopping for inside receiving work. I would ask Lavender to define that job before adding another target to a crowded idea of an offense.

prospects.name: Woobat
prospects.analysis: Woobat matches Gastly’s 41-inch vertical and 6.53 cone, with a 4.87 forty. The Icirrus prospect is 23 and level 23, carrying a 46–74 band. The test results justify a close look even though the present grade range sits below the leading group. I would rather discuss those specific strengths than dismiss the profile because it starts sixth.
prospects.concern: Seven bench reps and the lower grade band remain meaningful differences from stronger present candidates. Age 23 also gives less age-based runway than 21.
prospects.projection: A middle-board receiver to compare against actual openings, particularly for teams wanting movement help soon. I would keep him in Fortree’s comparison even if Meowth is unavailable.

prospects.name: Delibird
prospects.analysis: Lavaridge’s Delibird has the same 4.92 forty as Hulbury’s, with a 6.66 cone and eleven bench reps. The differences are the 42–70 band and 36-inch vertical. I like a prospect who keeps several useful measurements together. Being 21 is another reason to consider the longer view, provided a club can actually give him a useful development place.
prospects.concern: Level seven and the lower band make immediate starting assumptions unwise. A younger age does not award a future breakthrough.
prospects.projection: An option for a club building a receiving succession plan while retaining its current starter. Mossdeep has productive veterans and can afford to compare future jobs carefully.

prospects.name: Spinda
prospects.analysis: Gateon’s Spinda is my favorite of the four Spinda profiles in this group. The 4.90 forty, forty-inch vertical and 6.65 cone form the strongest movement combination among them, with thirteen bench reps as well. The 38–66 band is a reason to keep evaluating, not a reason to pretend the athletic differences are invisible.
prospects.concern: The band still reaches well below an assured starting standard. He must be compared as a whole player rather than selected because this is the best Spinda workout.
prospects.projection: A development-minded receiver target when the price reflects uncertainty. I would put him in Mossdeep’s longer-term comparison rather than promise an immediate role.

prospects.name: Spinda
prospects.analysis: Lavender Forest’s Spinda brings a 41–69 band and a 6.71 cone, but the five-second forty is slower than Gateon’s. There is a defensible argument for taking the stronger present band first. I lean the other way because I want the broader athletic package, and I am leaving this entry beside Gateon’s so that argument remains easy to have.
prospects.concern: At 23, there is less reason to pay a premium merely for youth. Nine bench reps and a 37-inch vertical do not separate him from the middle of the board.
prospects.projection: A receiver-needy team should compare the current evaluation directly with Gateon’s. A later selection makes more sense to me than reaching because the top of the band looks comfortable.

prospects.name: Spinda
prospects.analysis: I enjoy discussing Dewford University, and this Spinda gives me a respectable excuse. At 21, with a 37–65 band, a 38-inch vertical and a 6.80 cone, he belongs in the next group of developmental comparisons. I cannot honestly call the 4.95 forty exceptional. I can say the profile has more than one usable measurement.
prospects.concern: Eight bench reps and an uncertain current grade require a patient role. The university name is not a football skill, even when I like saying it.
prospects.projection: A later receiver option for a team with room to develop him. Fortree needs help, but it also needs to avoid confusing a pleasant school connection with readiness.

prospects.name: Ekans
prospects.analysis: Mesagoza State’s Ekans has a 38–66 band, a 4.95 forty and a 6.73 cone. Those numbers keep him close to the Spinda cluster. Eleven bench reps give him a useful strength result within that group. I would bring him into the comparison whenever the preferred receivers are gone and a club still has a specific job to fill.
prospects.concern: He is 23 and level six. Neither the band nor the 35-inch vertical supports a promise of immediate high-end receiving production.
prospects.projection: A later developmental option with a defined job, not a generic collection piece. Cerulean should compare him with the alternatives before assuming any receiver automatically fixes the offense.

prospects.name: Spinda
prospects.analysis: Fuji University’s Spinda closes the twelve with a 34–62 band, 4.98 forty and 6.77 cone. The cone time is close enough to the surrounding group to keep the discussion open. Ten bench reps and a 37-inch vertical complete a profile that needs a favorable price and a clear developmental purpose rather than a dramatic sales pitch.
prospects.concern: The lower end of the grade range is a substantial warning. I would not turn the similarities in testing into a claim that the receivers are interchangeable.
prospects.projection: A late comparison candidate for a club that can preserve a useful roster place. I would prioritize more complete receivers before making room for another uncertain project.

articles.title: What changed? A quarterback, two kickoffs and my Rustboro ranking
articles.dek: Mossdeep stays first. Mt. Silver faces a different future, Rustboro climbs twelve places, and Rowan keeps the receipts.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Mossdeep stays first. I am keeping Saffron second by the width of Venomoth’s escape route, with Sunyshore third and Mt. Silver fourth after the loss of Josh Alakazam. These are judgments about the teams facing next week, not a replacement standings table. The unbeaten Reds have every right to object.

The theme is what changed. Rustboro moved from twentieth to eighth because two 94-yard kickoff touchdowns and 222 rushing yards are difficult to ignore, even for someone whose previous ranking is now embarrassing. Every movement below compares with my published Week 5 list.

rankings.text: Four touchdowns for Ninjaskamara, zero punts for the offense and fifteen rushing yards allowed. The 41–3 win gives Mossdeep a plus-201 margin. I moved the Eclipse first last week and will now accept credit for noticing a fairly large object directly in front of me.

A 16–14 win at Fuchsia is an excellent way to make a ranking look like favoritism. The five sacks and Venomoth’s 69-yard touchdown kept the Psi Corps alive. I am retaining them here on the season’s 34 points allowed, with a stern look at zero third-down conversions.

Pat Serptain took a punt 63 yards for a touchdown, and Fred Whirler supplied a pick-six. Sunyshore won 34–7 after being last week’s return-story victim. The defense allowed 115 yards. I dislike how persuasive that is when I had prepared better jokes.

Six-and-oh deserves respect. Losing Josh Alakazam for the season requires a new forecast. Crem Ftzpatrik produced three touchdowns in relief, but Petalburg gets a week to prepare for him. Fourth is caution about the next game, not a retroactive deletion of the first six.

Eighteen carries, 108 yards and two rushing touchdowns in a 27–10 win. Dorian has already claimed personal responsibility. The passing game also supplied 221 yards, so Blaine appears to have discovered the legal right to use both parts of the playbook.

The Pride beat Mauville 21–9 and stand 5–1. A trip to unbeaten Mt. Silver now comes against an offense changing quarterbacks. This is a chance to earn a much louder place in the conversation. The Reds’ defense has not agreed to be accommodating.

Drakloak caught seven passes for 142 yards, Chandelure threw for 271, and Cerulean left with three points. At 4–1, the Volts have earned more attention. I am awarding it with the facial expression of someone paying a parking ticket.

My Way, Son returned two kickoffs 94 yards apiece and added 118 rushing yards in a 37–21 win. I had Rustboro twentieth. That receipt is ugly. So were Dewford’s coverage lanes. Parasect’s five-week absence keeps this from being an entirely carefree promotion.

I put Dewford fourth and then watched two Rustboro kickoff returns undo two enormous scoring plays. The Breakers still have useful wins, but zero-for-six on third down and three turnovers make the 37–21 defeat harder to shrug off than a single special-teams accident.

A bye kept Lavender at 4–1 with a plus-one margin. Mossdeep arrives next. This is rather like leaving a quiet room and discovering that the person waiting outside has scored ninety points in two games. A rested defense has a specific task.

The Dragons had a bye and remain 4–1 with a plus-one margin. Lavaridge comes next after scoring three points across two games. Blackthorn has collected close wins; this would be a considerate week to give its supporters a little more space.

Eterna led Snowpoint 24–7, allowed two late touchdowns and survived 24–21 after recovering the second onside kick. Slowking threw for 252 yards and three scores. That is a useful win with a final two minutes Gardenia should not frame.

Thirty-one to ten over Violet finally makes the plus-twenty scoring margin look a little less lonely beside a 2–4 record. The Frost have lost games they might have wanted back. This time they did the scoring early enough to keep the result.

The Bulwark held Oreburgh to 95 yards and won 13–6. Four-and-two still sits beside a minus-one margin, which is an awkward photograph. A trip to newly victorious Celadon will test whether Canalave can make another narrow advantage last.

Two late touchdowns and an onside recovery made a 24–7 deficit almost disappear. Almost remains a frustrating word at 2–4. The Blizzard have a plus-sixteen margin and another close loss. The standings office continues to insist on counting the losses.

Celadon got its first win at Viridian’s expense, 14–10. The Titans managed 139 yards and sixty-one through the air. A 3–3 record still leaves a route forward, but the next opponent is a Snowpoint team with its own complaint about close finishes.

Two consecutive wins have the Surge at 3–3. Delcatty caught seven for 152 yards in the 20–16 defeat of Fortree. The minus-forty season margin has not vanished, but the bye arrives after a much more useful pair of afternoons.

Last week Milotic got the cover. This week Mahogany supplied a 31–10 rebuttal. Violet falls to 2–4 and takes a bye. A spectacular trade-return story was a real event; apparently it did not include a subscription to future victories.

Mt. Silver won 27–7 even after changing quarterbacks. The Crushers did not score until 1:23 remained. At 2–4, Cianwood needs more than another explanation about a difficult opponent. Mauville offers a game it can reasonably be expected to win.

The Swarm followed their first win with a 17–14 victory at Olivine. Two-and-four is a long way from comfortable, but it is a considerable improvement on winless. Rustboro is next. I suggest remembering that the kickoff is part of the game.

A 17–14 win at Pastoria gives the Haunts a second victory. Frosmoth threw for 247 yards and Hearthome converted eight of fourteen third downs. This time the late possession ended with kneels rather than a new reason to discuss missed opportunities.

Pewter reached the end zone in Cinnabar and still lost 27–10. Four field goals had been enough the previous week; ten total points were not enough here. At 3–3, the Rockers get Oreburgh next and another chance to build an actual touchdown drive.

Five rushing yards, two interceptions and three points in Vermilion. The Tide are 3–3, but the offense has handed the next opponent a fairly direct list of targets. Sunyshore just held Veilstone to 115 yards. This is poor timing for another quiet afternoon.

A late touchdown was not enough to beat Azalea, which took the game 17–14. Olivine is 2–3 and hosts Dewford next. Both teams will arrive with a fresh reason to practice the part of football that happens after a promising moment.

Fourteen to ten over Viridian means the Bloom finally have a victory. Gholdengo threw two interceptions, but the defense held the Titans to 139 yards and the offense found a late rushing touchdown. One-and-five is a start, which is more than zero-and-five was.

One conversion in thirteen attempts, 115 total yards and a 34–7 defeat at Sunyshore. Veilstone is still 3–3 and still holds a playoff place today. A visit to Fuchsia will tell us whether the offense can produce more than a very generous interpretation of its record.

Hearthome won 17–14, leaving Pastoria 2–4 and heading into a bye. The Waves gained 189 yards. A fourth-quarter comeback is difficult to arrange when the other team can keep the ball and finish with kneels inside your five.

Petalburg won 21–9 and dropped the Dynamos to 2–4. The defense has allowed 122 points this season. A trip to Cianwood puts two teams with the same record together; at least one of them will have to find a more useful afternoon.

The narrow loss to Mt. Silver had made the Miners look dangerous. Ninety-five yards and six points against Canalave have complicated that sales pitch. Oreburgh is 1–5, with a visit to Pewter next. A touchdown would be a reasonable opening demand.

Saffron escaped 16–14. Empoleon completed 25 of thirty passes despite five sacks, and the Shadows scored twice in the fourth quarter. Still 0–6, but this was recognizably competitive football. Veilstone is next, and the opportunity is no longer difficult to explain.

The Skyhawks lost 20–16 at Sootopolis and Rabsca is listed out for a week. Fortree is 0–5. Mahogany has just scored 31, which makes finding a functioning passing plan more urgent than any argument about how close the last game was.

After the 48–0 loss came a 41–3 loss. Fifteen rushing yards and no third-down conversions in Mossdeep explain a great deal of it. The Inferno are 2–4, but these last two games require a repair more specific than remembering their two wins.

articles.title: Week 7: Petalburg tests the Reds, Lavender gets the Eclipse
articles.dek: Two unbeaten teams meet five-win and four-win challengers. Tessa grades her last slate and commits to all fourteen games.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: I went 10–5 in Week 6. Dorian went 12–3, Rowan and Mara each went 8–7, and Ellis went 7–8. I have checked the arithmetic twice in the hope it might make Dorian quieter. Across the two graded slates, Dorian leads at 20–9, followed by Rowan at 18–11, me at 17–12, Mara at 14–15 and Ellis at 12–17. The table below shows Week 6 alongside the season totals; shared closest-score bonuses remain separate from the win-loss records.

Three checks from last week are worth revisiting. Mossdeep hit both of my home keys: Lavaridge had zero third-down conversions and Marino took zero sacks. Saffron got the three sacks I asked for and two more, but lost a fumble and nearly the game. Sunyshore lost no fumbles yet converted only three of nine third downs; the returns and defense supplied a comfortable win anyway. A useful key can explain part of a game without being an automatic formula for the result.

The two biggest Week 7 tests are Petalburg at Mt. Silver and Mossdeep at Lavender. One undefeated team has a new quarterback; the other meets a rested 4–1 opponent. Saffron, Violet, Sootopolis and Pastoria have byes. Fourteen games leave seventy panel picks below, with every score saved before kickoff.

matchups.matchup: Snowpoint’s passing finish against Viridian’s stalled offense
matchups.analysis: Snowpoint made a 24–7 deficit into a 24–21 finish, but the comeback began too late. Viridian gained only 139 yards against Celadon. I prefer the Blizzard’s ability to create scores, provided they do not wait until the final two minutes to demonstrate it. The Titans need more than another efficient stretch from Gabite to keep pace.
matchups.awayKey: Score two touchdowns before the fourth quarter and lose no fumbles.
matchups.homeKey: Reach 150 passing yards and hold Snowpoint below three touchdowns.

matchups.matchup: Two offenses looking for a second way to score
matchups.analysis: Oreburgh gained 95 yards in Canalave. Pewter scored ten in Cinnabar after winning the previous week entirely through kicks. This is an invitation to choose the home defense and keep the score modest. The Miners can change that calculation by sustaining even a couple of drives; I am not treating a close loss to Mt. Silver two weeks ago as permanent proof.
matchups.awayKey: Convert at least four third downs and score a touchdown.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Oreburgh below 200 yards and finish two scoring drives.

matchups.matchup: Slowking’s clean pocket against Cinnabar’s renewed balance
matchups.analysis: Eterna’s Slowking threw three touchdowns without taking a sack at Snowpoint. Cinnabar ran for 108 yards and protected Gholdengo to one sack against Pewter. That gives this game two plausible offensive paths. I lean toward the Blaze at home, but Eterna’s passing protection makes the margin small enough to discuss without theatrics. Dorian will supply those anyway.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than one sack and complete two touchdown passes.
matchups.homeKey: Run for at least ninety yards and avoid a negative turnover margin.

matchups.matchup: Canalave’s possession game against a newly confident defense
matchups.analysis: Celadon’s first win came while holding Viridian to 139 yards. Canalave held Oreburgh to 95 and won with 116 rushing yards. I expect a close game built from ordinary gains rather than fireworks. The Bloom can absolutely win it; I give the Bulwark a narrow edge because their run game has just shown a way to finish a one-score game with the ball.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for one hundred yards and lose no fumbles.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Canalave under twenty and throw no more than one interception.

matchups.matchup: Empoleon’s quick completions against Veilstone’s reset
matchups.analysis: I am picking the winless team. Fuchsia completed 25 of thirty passes against Saffron and scored twice late. Veilstone converted one of thirteen third downs in Sunyshore. Neither performance guarantees the next, but the Shadows showed more usable offense. Reducing the five sacks from last week would give those completions a much better chance to matter before the fourth quarter.
matchups.awayKey: Convert four third downs and allow no return touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Take no more than two sacks and score a touchdown before halftime.

matchups.matchup: Drakloak’s production against the Haunts’ undermanned secondary
matchups.analysis: Drakloak caught seven for 142 in Vermilion’s win. Hearthome has just won at Pastoria but still has Palafin listed out for a week. The Haunts can sustain drives, as eight third-down conversions showed, and that is their route to keeping the ball away. I prefer the Volts’ passing attack against a defense that has more work to do than the final 17–14 score suggests.
matchups.awayKey: Convert at least half the third downs and allow fewer than two sacks.
matchups.homeKey: Give up no passing touchdowns of thirty yards or more and reach 250 passing yards.

matchups.matchup: Sunyshore’s pressure against a struggling Tide attack
matchups.analysis: Cerulean scored three points, rushed for five yards and threw two interceptions at Vermilion. Sunyshore just forced two interceptions and four sacks. That is a severe matchup on the current evidence. The Starseekers still need better third-down offense than three-for-nine, but their defense gives them time to find it. The Tide must make an ordinary sustained drive available early.
matchups.awayKey: Take the ball away twice and convert at least four third downs.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no more than two sacks and rush for at least sixty yards.

matchups.matchup: Gardevoir’s response after a late-only touchdown
matchups.analysis: Both teams are 2–4. Mauville scored nine against Petalburg; Cianwood did not score against Mt. Silver until 1:23 remained. I give the Crushers a home edge and expect their rushing game to provide the steadier opening. Gardevoir needs completions that move possessions while the game is still within reach. Another touchdown after the result is settled will not answer that demand.
matchups.awayKey: Finish two touchdown drives and lose no fumbles.
matchups.homeKey: Score before halftime and hold Mauville below 250 total yards.

matchups.matchup: Dewford’s third-down repair against Olivine’s pass rush
matchups.analysis: The Breakers were zero-for-six on third down in the Rustboro loss. Olivine sacked Azalea’s Drampa six times and still lost 17–14. That creates a direct test of Dewford’s ability to avoid the most obvious passing situations. I still favor the visitors narrowly, while acknowledging that I favored them rather more confidently last week and got two kickoff returns thrown at the prediction.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no return touchdown and convert at least four third downs.
matchups.homeKey: Record three sacks and commit no turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Petalburg gets the first full week to prepare for Crem
matchups.analysis: Mt. Silver’s record is 6–0, but the offense now faces life without Josh Alakazam as well as the continuing absence of Garshawn Lynch. Crem Ftzpatrik’s relief performance was good enough to win comfortably. Petalburg is 5–1 and has just held Mauville to nine. I am choosing the Reds’ defense in a close game, with the new quarterback asked to keep mistakes small.
matchups.awayKey: Hold Mt. Silver below 100 rushing yards and force two turnovers.
matchups.homeKey: Lose no fumbles and keep Petalburg below twenty-one points.

matchups.matchup: Rustboro’s rushing depth against a two-win Swarm streak
matchups.analysis: My Way, Son and Philly combined for 198 rushing yards in Dewford. Azalea has won twice in succession, so this is not a convenient place for Rustboro to assume the next victory will arrive with the kickoff. I like the Stone’s ground game even without another return score. Parasect’s five-week absence gives the Swarm a reason to test the middle of the defense.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 150 yards and lose no fumbles.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no return touchdown and complete two touchdown passes.

matchups.matchup: Fortree’s quarterback problem against a thawing Frost offense
matchups.analysis: Rabsca is listed out for a week after Fortree’s 20–16 loss at Sootopolis. Mahogany has just beaten Violet 31–10. The Frost’s 2–4 record still understates the plus-twenty scoring margin, but this is a chance to make the record less argumentative. Fortree needs a workable passing day and enough possession to stop the game becoming a chase.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than two sacks and score before halftime.
matchups.homeKey: Score at least three touchdowns and keep Fortree below 250 yards.

matchups.matchup: Lavaridge’s run game against another difficult road assignment
matchups.analysis: The Inferno have scored three points across two games and gained fifteen rushing yards in Mossdeep. Blackthorn returns from a bye at 4–1. I do not need to invent a much larger gap in talent to favor the rested home side. Lavaridge has to establish some modest rushing success and finish a possession; Blackthorn should make it earn the entire field.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for sixty yards and convert at least four third downs.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no offensive play of forty yards and lose no fumbles.

matchups.matchup: A rested Lavender defense against Ninjaskamara in two roles
matchups.analysis: Mossdeep arrives 6–0 after a 41–3 win with no punts. Lavender is 4–1 after its bye, but its season scoring margin is only plus-one. The Wails need to end possessions and prevent the halfback from becoming a deep receiver behind them. I favor the Eclipse. My check is whether Lavender can force three punts; if it can, the game has a chance to stay within one late score.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than one sack and finish three touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Force three punts and allow no completion of thirty yards or more.
